name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,147

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A French poet – chap eating garlic?

indicators.note: whatever eats something takes it inside, so one piece is swallowed by the other

blocks.note: a chap is a man, a male
garlic is one example of a herb, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: A Frenchman known for verse, pictured as a fellow munching garlic.
explanation.walkthrough: François de Malherbe (1555-1628) was a French poet and critic; his name even means 'bad herb' in French, which the garlic joke nods to.
explanation.definitionFit: Malherbe was a court poet under Henri IV and a reformer of French verse, so he is a French poet.

clue.text: A flash of French style

blocks.note: 'half a mo' or 'just a mo': a mo is a moment, a flash
de is French for 'of'

explanation.surface: A sudden burst of Gallic chic.
explanation.walkthrough: MO is British slang for a moment, as in 'wait a mo'. 'French' tells you to translate the little word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A mode is a prevailing fashion or manner, so it is another word for a style.

clue.text: Secure, from approval in this ancient religious tract …

blocks.note: to secure a job or a fish is to land it
'of' can mean 'from', as in a man of Kent
a nod signals approval

explanation.surface: Someone wins endorsement for an old religious pamphlet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tract' suggests a religious pamphlet, but here it means a stretch of land. The ellipsis carries 'this' over to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Genesis says Cain went to dwell in a region east of Eden, so it is a biblical stretch of territory from ancient scripture.

clue.text: … and this Roman moral standard

blocks.note: et is Latin for 'and'; 'Roman' asks for Latin
hic is Latin for 'this'

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a Roman principle of conduct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman' looks like it describes the standard, but it asks you to put both little words into Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethic is a principle of right conduct, so it is a guiding rule of morality.

clue.text: Kit in certain London tearooms, one described in Dombey and Son

definitions.text: one described in Dombey and Son

blocks.note: first meaning, spaced differently: the kettles belonging to a north London borough

blocks.clueFragment: one described in Dombey and Son
blocks.note: second meaning: a pompous MP whose family young Paul Dombey visits in the Dickens novel

explanation.surface: Equipment in some London cafés, and a figure from Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet is a borough of north London. Read the name with the space moved one letter left and the Dickens character becomes kettles owned by that borough.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Barnet Skettles is a pompous MP whose household young Paul Dombey visits in Dickens's novel.

clue.text: Trance induced by Proust translation

indicators.note: a translation renders text into another form, so the letters are carried over into a new order

blocks.note: the French novelist's name taken as written

explanation.surface: Reading Proust in English sends you into a daze.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke is that Proust's very long novel puts its readers to sleep; 'translation' is not about language here.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a dazed state of near unconsciousness, close in sense to a trance.

clue.text: The weird sister – Shakespeare character who talks of raising devils

definitions.text: Shakespeare character who talks of raising devils

indicators.note: something weird is strange and out of shape, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, after the mixing signal

explanation.surface: Macbeth's weird sisters, the witches, are evoked before a character who speaks of conjuring devils.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The weird sister' points to the witches in Macbeth, but the play wanted is Troilus and Cressida; 'weird' sits inside the words it rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Thersites, the railing Greek in Troilus and Cressida, says he will 'learn to conjure and raise devils' to see his curses work.

clue.text: Favourite god of Heliopolis, a Middle Eastern city

blocks.note: a pet is a favourite, as in teacher's pet
Ra, the Egyptian sun god, was worshipped at Heliopolis

explanation.surface: The best-loved deity of an Egyptian city.
explanation.walkthrough: Heliopolis looks like the city to find, but it only places the sun god; the answer is a different city.
explanation.definitionFit: Petra is the ancient rock-cut Nabataean city in Jordan, a Middle Eastern site.

clue.text: Bitter spinster, showing low cunning in part

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so these pieces go within another

blocks.note: an actor's part is a role
feeling low is feeling sad
art can mean craft or cunning, as in artful

explanation.surface: A sour unmarried woman revealing a little sly deviousness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In part' reads like 'partly', but 'part' is a role and the gloom and craft go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: In David Copperfield, Mrs Steerforth's scarred, unmarried companion is consumed by resentment and jealousy, a bitter spinster.

clue.text: Dick travelled North to consume everything in a cocktail

indicators.note: what consumes something takes it inside, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: rode means travelled on horseback or by vehicle
a rickey is a cocktail of spirit, lime and soda, as in gin rickey
all means everything
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Someone called Dick headed north to drink a whole cocktail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dick' looks like a man's name but is slang for a detective. North's letter comes last though it is named first.
explanation.definitionFit: Roderick Alleyn is Ngaio Marsh's Scotland Yard detective, and dick is old slang for a private eye or police investigator.

clue.text: In hand-shaking I identify Morris the preacher

indicators.note: something shaken is jumbled about, so its letters are mixed into a new order
placed at the front, this word says the next piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: On shaking someone's hand I recognise a preacher named Morris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hand-shaking' reads as a greeting, but the hyphen hides a word followed by its own mixing signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Dinah Morris is the Methodist woman preacher in George Eliot's novel Adam Bede.

clue.text: Put Lawrence and Muslim back in restricted quarters

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the string runs right to left

blocks.note: to put something down is to set it
T. E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia
the Moors were Muslims of North Africa and Spain

explanation.surface: Lawrence of Arabia and a Muslim companion are sent back to cramped lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lawrence' is not D. H. but T. E., known by his initials.
explanation.definitionFit: A roomette is a small private sleeping compartment on a train, so roomettes are cramped accommodation.

clue.text: Study a Mediterranean location, and its description by J.G. Ballard

definitions.note: names the author; the answer is his novel

blocks.note: to con is to study or pore over
Crete is a Mediterranean island
what that location is, described

explanation.surface: Examine a Mediterranean place and Ballard's account of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Its description' points back to the place just found: describe it by what kind of place it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballard wrote a 1974 novel about a man stranded on waste ground between motorways, under that title.

clue.text: Kings associated with ambassadors and a princess

definitions.text: associated with ambassadors and a princess
definitions.note: a description of the novelist, not a noun

blocks.note: a name borne by eight English kings
a name borne by two English kings and several Scottish ones; the plural asks for two

explanation.surface: Monarchs mixing with diplomats and royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: The ambassadors and princess are not courtiers but novels: The Ambassadors and The Princess Casamassima.
explanation.definitionFit: The American-born novelist wrote both The Ambassadors and The Princess Casamassima, so he is the writer tied to those titles.

clue.text: Germaine’s female, and Terence’s male

definitions.note: singular; the answer is plural because the two meanings together make two
singular; the answer is plural because the two meanings together make two

blocks.note: first meaning: the title figure of Germaine Greer's 1970 feminist book
second meaning: the title figure of the Roman playwright Terence's comedy Eunuchus

explanation.surface: One person's woman and another person's man.
explanation.walkthrough: Germaine Greer wrote The Female Eunuch; the Roman playwright Terence wrote a comedy called Eunuchus. Each title supplies one, hence the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Greer's title figure and Terence's title figure are both castrated or emasculated people, so together they make two of them.

clue.text: Webster, possibly a friend of Wilbur in a 22 work

definitions.text: a friend of Wilbur in a 22 work

blocks.note: first meaning: a spider, a maker of webs, or perhaps a woman surnamed Webster

blocks.clueFragment: a friend of Wilbur in a 22 work
blocks.note: second meaning: the spider who befriends Wilbur the pig in E. B. White's children's book

explanation.walkthrough: Webster looks like the dictionary maker, but read it as 'one who makes webs'. 22 is WHITE, and the book is Charlotte's Web.
explanation.definitionFit: The spider heroine of E. B. White's 1952 book saves Wilbur the pig by spinning words into her web.

clue.text: He, thee and me could make 18, 3 or something similar

blocks.note: surface reading: a group of three people getting together

blocks.clueFragment: He, thee and me could make
blocks.note: setter's reading: three persons add up to the number three, a whole number like eighteen

explanation.surface: Three people could between them produce a couple of numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: '18, 3' look like cross-references to other clues, but they are just numbers; three people make three, which is one more such number.
explanation.definitionFit: Eighteen and three are whole numbers with no fractional part, which is what mathematicians call this kind of number.

clue.text: Waterspouts ascending torment Jerome’s idle sea captain

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to rag is to tease or torment
Captain Goyles, the yarn-spinning sea captain in Jerome K. Jerome's Novel Notes, serialised in his magazine The Idler

explanation.surface: Rising waterspouts plague a lazy sea captain from Jerome K. Jerome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waterspouts' suggests weather at sea alongside the captain, but it is the definition, meaning the carved spouts on church gutters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gargoyles are grotesque carved stone spouts that throw rainwater clear of a building's walls.

clue.text: Revolutionary band’s administration

blocks.note: a red is a revolutionary communist
a tape is a narrow band of material

explanation.surface: The government of a rebel group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' suggests a group of people, but here it is a strip of material.
explanation.definitionFit: Red tape is excessive bureaucratic procedure, the paperwork side of officialdom and administration.

clue.text: Bird – she takes Trelawney’s heart

indicators.note: a heart is the core of something, so the letters wanted lie inside the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A woman captures Trelawney's affections.
explanation.walkthrough: Trelawney suggests a literary character to look up, but the name only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A kestrel is a small falcon that hovers over open ground, so it is a bird of prey.

clue.text: A lady with timber in short supply, but one who ran a famous workshop

definitions.text: one who ran a famous workshop

blocks.note: Joan is a woman's name
timber in short supply is little wood

explanation.surface: A woman short of wood nonetheless ran a well-known workshop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Workshop' suggests carpentry, matching the timber, but it is a theatre company.
explanation.definitionFit: Joan Littlewood founded and directed Theatre Workshop at Stratford East, staging Oh, What a Lovely War!

clue.text: One crossing a foreign river was a legendary poet

indicators.note: to cross something is to pass through its middle, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: the Aron is a river in Burgundy, France
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone who forded a river abroad turned out to be a famous bard.
explanation.walkthrough: The river is a minor French tributary of the Loire, not one most solvers know.
explanation.definitionFit: Arion was a Greek lyric poet of legend, saved from drowning by a dolphin charmed by his music.

clue.text: Like some knights, or one who wrote about them

blocks.note: first meaning: the colour of chivalrous rescuing knights and of one side's chess pieces
second meaning: the author of The Once and Future King, about Arthur's knights

explanation.walkthrough: The same word serves as an adjective for knights and as the surname of their chronicler; 'them' links the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Heroic rescuers are called by that colour of knight, and T. H. White retold the Arthurian legends.

clue.text: Ted’s tough kind of man – or woman

definitions.text: Ted’s tough kind of man – or woman

blocks.clueFragment: Ted’s tough kind of man – or woman
blocks.note: surface reading: someone called Ted likes hard men or hard women

blocks.clueFragment: Ted’s tough kind of man – or woman
blocks.note: setter's reading: Ted Hughes wrote a children's story about a metal giant and a sequel about a metal woman

explanation.walkthrough: Ted is the poet Ted Hughes, whose The Iron Man (1968) was followed by The Iron Woman (1993).
explanation.definitionFit: The metal in both of Hughes's titles also describes someone tough and unyielding, as in an iron will.

clue.text: Principal subject of the Hornblower series?

definitions.text: Principal subject of the Hornblower series?

blocks.note: surface reading: the chief topic running through a series of novels
setter's reading: C. S. Forester's naval novels are about the sea, which old poetry calls 'the main'

explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old word for the open sea, as in the Spanish Main; Hornblower is Forester's Napoleonic naval officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means the central subject of a work, and here the subject is also literally the ocean.

clue.text: “Belief in progress is a doctrine of –s and Belgians” (Baudelaire, translated by Isherwood)

definitions.text: “Belief in progress is a doctrine of –s and Belgians” (Baudelaire, translated by Isherwood)

blocks.clueFragment: “Belief in progress is a doctrine of –s and Belgians”
blocks.note: the quotation with one word removed
the source: Isherwood's English version of Baudelaire's journals, Intimate Journals

explanation.walkthrough: The blank is the missing word in Baudelaire's jibe, from Isherwood's translation of his Intimate Journals; the grid wants it singular.
explanation.definitionFit: Baudelaire mocks faith in progress as a creed for lazy people who expect improvement without effort.

clue.text: The final event at Blandings

blocks.note: surface reading: the last thing to happen at Lord Emsworth's castle in Wodehouse
setter's reading: the end of the day, and the title of Wodehouse's last, unfinished Blandings novel

explanation.walkthrough: P. G. Wodehouse died while writing Sunset at Blandings (1977), so the end of the day was also the end of the series.
explanation.definitionFit: The going down of the sun is the last event of each day, and it names Wodehouse's final novel.

clue.text: Job – for a mutinous sailor in Treasure Island

definitions.text: a mutinous sailor in Treasure Island

blocks.note: surface reading: a post or task meant for somebody

blocks.clueFragment: Job – for a mutinous sailor in Treasure Island
blocks.note: setter's reading: Job is the first name of a pirate, and the dash asks for his surname

explanation.walkthrough: 'Job' looks like work, but it is the first name of the boatswain who joins Long John Silver's mutiny in Stevenson's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Job Anderson, the Hispaniola's boatswain, is a ringleader of Silver's rebellious crew in Stevenson's story.
